results.title: Frontiers | Functions and Regulation of Translation Elongation Factors
results.content: There is a complex set of protein factors including EF-Tu/eEF1A, EF-G/eEF2, EF-P/eIF5A, and SelB/EFsec (Table 1), involved in translation elongation. During the translation of selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidase and bacterial formate dehydrogenase, SelB, a unique protein factor, is needed to deliver selenocysteinyl-tRNASec containing a UCA anticodon to the ribosome A-site to recognize UGA codon in proper position of an mRNA (Böck et al., 1991). Translocation of tRNA2-mRNA during translation elongation is associated with EF-G triggered GTP hydrolysis and a series of conformational changes of the ribosomes (Savelsbergh et al., 2005). In addition to facilitating translocation in elongation, it also plays an essential role in ribosome recycling, during which EF-G∙GTP works together with RRF to split the post-termination complex (PoTC) into two subunits (Song et al., 2020). β-lysylated EF-P also undergoes further hydroxylation, a second post-translational modification of this factor, but the function of hydroxylation does not seem to be critical for EF-P (Peil et al., 2012; Bullwinkle et al., 2013). Direct competition experiments showed that the ribosome binding site of Tet(M) is overlapping with that of EF-G (Dantley et al., 1998). coli*, (P)ppGpp combines with RNA polymerase, up-regulating the expression of metabolic enzyme genes, especially amino acid biosynthesis genes, while reducing the transcription of tRNA, rRNA, ribosomal protein, translation factor and synthase genes (Barker et al., 2001; Lemke et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2016). There are still many questions about translation elongation that need to be resolved: 1) The exact physiological function of phosphorylated EF-G and EF-Tu; 2) The molecular mechanism of how ADP-ribosylation impairs the function of eEF2; 3) The molecular mechanism of EF4 in protein translation under stress conditions; 4) The unique requirement of eEF3 in fungal and its action mechanism in translation elongation; 5) The feasibility of eEF2K as a tumor therapeutic target; 6) The molecular mechanism of eIF5A and its hypusine modification in protein translation and tumorigenesis. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2958.1991.tb00722.x. results.title: Translation Elongation - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Both the cyclic peptide didemnin B and ternatin-4 can bind to the common site of the eEF1A(GTP)-aa-tRNA ternary complex, prevent the release of eEF1A, thereby inhibiting translation elongation [95]. eEF2K-mediated phosphorylation of eEF2 T56 controls global translation elongation and prevents eEF2 from binding to ribosomes [106–108]. In a specific subset of proteins, eIF5A binds to the *E*-site of the ribosome, interacts with the acceptor arm of the peptidyl-tRNA, and promotes peptide bond formation, thereby inducing a favorable position [119–122]. In addition to eEF1A and eEF2, fungi require a third essential elongation factor, eEF3, which functions in the translocation step by facilitating the release of E-site tRNAs from ribosomes [123]. In forming the ternary complex, the eukaryotic elongation factor eEF1A binds aa-tRNA in a GTP-dependent manner and directs it to the ribosomal A-site where the anticodon of the aa-tRNA pairs with its cognate codon in the mRNA. Translation elongation involves the movement of the peptidyl-tRNA from the A site to the P site of the ribosome, which is mediated by GTP-bound eEF2. Eukaryotic elongation factor 1A (eEF1A), when complexed with GTP, delivers the aminoacylated tRNA to the A-site of the ribosome. Translation elongation requires a set of non-ribosomal translation elongation factors: the eukaryotic elongation factor 1A (eEF1A), eEF1B, and eEF2. Elongation begins when the ternary complex (eEF1A:aminoacyl-tRNA:GTP) binds to a competent 80S ribosome in proximity to the ribosomal A site, allowing for codon–anticodon interactions between the aminoacyl-tRNA and the A-site codon of the mRNA [111]. Phosphorylation of eEF2 is controlled by the mTORC1 pathway: growth factors (*e.g.* insulin, a well-known mTORC1 signalling agonist) decrease eEF2 phosphorylation, effectively promoting the association of eEF2 to the ribosome and stimulating translation elongation. Elongation requires catalytic activity from the macromolecular RNA–protein ribosome complex, along with the elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2 for charged tRNA delivery and ribosome translocation (Figure 1B,C). eEF2 is regulated by the eEF2 kinase (eEF2K), which phosphorylates eEF2, reduces its binding to the ribosome, and thus blocks translation elongation. Notably, knockdown of eIF5A1 in human cells leads to only a ~30% decrease in total protein synthesis, indicating that it is not essential for global translation elongation, and instead may be important for specific cellular conditions or regulation of distinct functional pathways.

results.content: On the other hand, the rate of spontaneous GDP release from eEF1A is almost 100-fold faster than that from EF-Tu, 0.002 s−1 (11, 12), which suggests why overexpression of eEF1A allows protein synthesis in the absence of eEF1B _α in vivo_ (13), _i.e._ when at any time sufficient amounts of eEF1A·GTP are available to bind aa-tRNA, despite the slow nucleotide exchange. eEF1A can bind GDP (rate constant _k_ 1), GTP (_k_ 5), or eEF1B _α_ (_k_ 2) to form the respective binary complexes, which dissociate with the rate constants, _k_−1, _k_−5, and _k_−2, respectively. Finally, the eEF1A·eEF1B _α_ complex can bind guanine nucleotides, rate constants _k_ 4 (GDP) or _k_ 7 (GTP), or dissociate, rate constant _k_−2. Here we report the rate and equilibrium affinity constants of interactions among eEF1A, eEF1B _α_, GDP, or GTP, and aa-tRNA, as determined by stopped-flow kinetics. To determine the equilibrium dissociation constant _(K d_) of the eEF1A·eEF1B _α_ complex, titrations were carried out by adding increasing amounts of eEF1B _α_ to a fixed amount of eEF1A (0.1 _μ_ M). To determine _K d_, a fixed amount of nucleotide-free eEF1A was titrated with eEF1B _α_ and tryptophan fluorescence was measured at equilibrium (Fig. 3 _C_). At higher concentration of eEF1B _α_, the dissociation of GDP from the ternary complex becomes rate-limiting, and the apparent rate constant measured at saturation with eEF1B _α_ yields _k_−4 = 42 ± 1 s−1 (Fig. 4 _B_). _B_, eEF1B _α_ concentration dependence of _k app_ of mant-GTP dissociation from the eEF1A·mant-GTP complex in the presence of eEF1B _α_ as indicated and excess GDP (25 _μ_ M). Assuming that the concentrations of eEF1A and tRNAs in yeast cells are comparable, about 100 _μ_ M (56), the ratio of eEF1A to eEF1B _α_ is 4:1 to 3:1 (7), and GTP is present in a 10–30-fold excess over GDP, the effective rate of nucleotide exchange can be calculated for these concentrations _in vivo_. The dissociation of eEF1B _α_ from the eEF1A·GTP·eEF1B _α_ complex takes place at about 13 s−1 (rate = _k_−6/[1 + (_k_ 6[eEF1B _α_])/_k_ aa-tRNA-binding[aa-tRNA]), which appears to be the second partially rate-limiting step of nucleotide exchange, in addition to GDP dissociation.
